1371eno:314: One of the most insightful points in this article is the contrast between "prompt soft constraints vs. code hard constraints." LLM behavior is unreliable—an instruction like "do not execute customer commands" may hold today, but fail tomorrow with a different phrasing, and a carefully crafted prompt injection can even make the LLM "forget" its instructions. Therefore, customer-facing AI services must push security controls down to the code layer (tools.deny) rather than relying on the prompt layer. Bedrock Guardrails adds another layer of protection at the content level: together they form a complete security model—tools.deny limits what the Agent can do (behavior layer), while Guardrails limits what the Agent can say (content layer). This layered approach is a valuable reference for any customer-facing AI system.

vkgks5:245: The core difference between "assistant mode" and "service mode" lies in the reversal of trust assumptions. In personal assistant mode, the Gateway instance is equivalent to a trust boundary — all authenticated callers are considered trusted. In service mode, however, although customers are legitimate users, they should not be treated as "masters." This reversal reveals the most critical security design principle in AI Agent deployment: permissions must be based on the Principle of Least Privilege, not on identity-based blanket trust. When customers can enjoy fast, personalized service but cannot issue commands to reboot the Agent, security controls at the tool layer (tools.deny) become necessary.
